idiom_name: LINQ deferred execution over IEnumerable<T> (yield-return iterators); IAsyncEnumerable<T> for async streams
implementation_notes: System.Linq is the platform's fusion story: query operators such as Where and Select are implemented with deferred execution - the immediate return value stores the query and nothing is executed until the object is enumerated - so a Select/Where/Sum chain streams element by element with no intermediate List, and the C# compiler builds the per-stage state machines from iterator methods (yield return). Terminal operations (ToList, ToArray, Count, Sum, foreach) are the explicit materialization points, and IAsyncEnumerable<T> with await foreach gives the same streaming shape for asynchronous sources. Providers implementing IQueryable push the whole chain into the target system, where the query planner performs the actual fusion instead of returning one result set per operator.
pitfalls: Deferred execution re-runs the whole chain on every enumeration: enumerating an IEnumerable twice queries twice unless you materialize once with ToList/ToArray.
Closures in a lazy chain run at enumeration time, so a captured variable mutated in between is read late - a classic aliasing bug.
LINQ-to-objects adds an iterator state machine and a delegate call per element; in hot loops over small arrays a plain for loop or span is faster.
